This paper presents the theory, the data infrastructure, and the pre-registered estimation protocol of the welfare-gate project. Estimation is implemented in Python on public Our World in Data panels; results from the pre-registered specifications will be reported in the companion empirical paper.*\n\n## Abstract\n\nThe literature on democratic erosion in the twenty-first century holds two contradictory accounts. The materialist account finds that income inequality is among the strongest predictors of democratic decline [1, 2]. The coalitional account argues, from close case comparison, that economic grievances did not systematically distinguish post-1990 backsliders from survivors [3]. This paper argues that the contradiction is unresolved because neither side tests the conditioning structure: neither asks whether the inequality-to-erosion link is institutionally gated. We develop the welfare-gate hypothesis. Among post-1990 democratizers, rising income inequality erodes liberal democracy only where welfare institutions are thin. In countries whose first democratic decade built strong universal public services, public health and education systems that the broad middle class uses, inequality surges do not transmit into subsequent declines in the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index three to five years later; where welfare institutions stayed thin, the same surges predict graded erosion. Three mechanisms compose the gate: automatic stabilization, which absorbs market-income shocks before they reach the distribution citizens experience; constituency formation through policy feedback, which gives the middle class a material stake in the public institutions that erosion would capture; and credible pre-commitment, which blocks the populist-promise equilibrium through which elites respond to redistributive threats by starving redistribution [11]. The gate also explains the co-evolution of inequality, education, and democratic quality: the inequality-reduction leg of the democratic dividend [10] materializes only behind strong welfare institutions, and the size of the first-decade dividend predicts resilience two decades later. The corollary is that welfare generosity bought later by incumbents, targeted cash or chauvinist transfers, does not gate. The full research design, including the pre-committed falsification criteria and the exact specifications to be estimated, is presented here; all variables are drawn from public Our World in Data panels, and the analysis is fully reproducible.\n\n## 1. Introduction\n\nSince the mid-1990s, the main threat to democracy has no longer been the military coup. It is the power-aggrandizing elected executive: presidents and prime ministers who harass the press, capture courts, and de-legitimize elections [4, 5]. Scholars now speak of a third wave of autocratization, and of erosion as a graded, incremental process inside formally democratic regimes rather than a discrete breakdown [4, 6, 7]. The phenomenon runs from national executives down to subnational governments [8]. This shift in the form of the threat has forced a shift in explanation. The old question, what kills democracies, has given way to a new one: what determines how much democratic quality a regime loses, and which democracies lose almost none?\n\nTwo answers currently compete. The materialist account points to economic inequality. Across a large cross-national sample of uninterrupted democracies for 1995-2020, Rau and Stokes find that the post-tax Gini coefficient is one of the strongest predictors of the onset of democratic erosion, robust across more than one hundred model specifications and immune to reverse-causation tests [1]. The finding extends an older result: in the coup era, inequality harmed democratic consolidation even where it did not block democratization [2], in line with the canonical political-economy tradition in which distributional conflict drives regime outcomes [8, 9, 15]. The coalitional account pushes back. From close comparison of the post-1990 wave, Haggard and Kaufman conclude that economic grievances and rising inequality did not systematically separate the backsliders from the resilient; polarization and elite coalitional choices did [3, 14, 32]. One body of work says inequality is a, perhaps the, driver of erosion. Another says the economic story fails exactly in the cases that matter.\n\nBoth cannot be right in the unconditional form in which they are stated, and this paper argues that the dispute has not been resolved because neither side has run the design that could resolve it. The global statistical account estimates a main effect. Its specifications contain no welfare-state variables, no education variables, and no moderators, and its sample of uninterrupted democracies excludes precisely the young post-1990 democratizers that fell below the democracy threshold while eroding [1]. The case-based account compares backsliders with survivors but never formalizes the interaction structure that a conditional claim requires [3]. What is missing in both is the institutional environment: the welfare state. The democratic-dividend literature supplies the missing prior. Democratization raises tax revenues and schooling but has no robust average effect on inequality [10]; the effect is heterogeneous, and the heterogeneity is unexplained. Acemoglu, Egorov, and Sonin show that when voters fear politicians are captured by the rich, redistributive promises become electorally decisive, and populist equilibria emerge [11]. Put the two results together with the welfare-state literature, and a precise conditional structure emerges. The welfare state is the institutional gate that determines whether an inequality shock reaches democratic institutions at all.\n\nWe state the hypothesis plainly. Among post-1990 democratizers, rising income inequality erodes democratic quality only where welfare institutions are weak. Countries whose first democratic decade built universal public services, health and education systems that the broad middle class uses, are insulated: inequality surges do not translate into declines in the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index three to five years later. Countries whose welfare institutions stayed thin experience the full transmission of inequality shocks into graded erosion. Three mechanisms compose the gate: automatic stabilization, by which universal services absorb market-income shocks before they reach the distribution citizens experience; constituency formation through policy feedback, by which the middle class acquires a material stake in the very institutions that erosion would capture; and credible pre-commitment, by which universal automatic programs block the endogenous-limits-to-redistribution path that feeds populist equilibria. The gate also explains the co-evolution of inequality, education, and democracy: the inequality-reduction leg of the democratic dividend materializes only where welfare institutions are strong, education expands into absorbed middle-class employment only there, and the size of the first-decade dividend predicts resilience two decades later.\n\nThe design exploits a natural experiment of sorts. The post-1990 democratization wave (transitions 1989-2005 in the Regimes of the World and Boix-Miller-Rosato classifications) provides quasi-exogenous transition timing [12, 13]. Welfare legacies at the moment of transition, communist-era health and education systems in Eastern Europe, colonial-era public services elsewhere, were inherited rather than chosen by the new democracies. The hypothesis is thus testable on an Our World in Data country-year panel from 1990 to 2022, with no external data, no expert-coding, and no proprietary sources. We fix the pre-registered protocol, the exact specifications, and the falsification criteria in Section 6, before any estimation.\n\n[FIGURE:fig1]\n\nThe paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 lays out the two accounts and the missing interaction. Section 3 develops the theory of the welfare gate and derives five testable hypotheses. Section 4 describes the data and measurement, all drawn from public panels. Section 5 details the estimation strategy. Section 6 states the pre-committed confirmation and disconfirmation criteria. Section 7 discusses what each pattern of findings would mean for the literature, Section 8 confronts the limitations, and Section 9 concludes.\n\n**Summary of contributions.** (i) We reconcile the materialist and coalitional accounts of post-1990 democratic erosion by identifying the institutional condition under which each holds: inequality erodes democracy where welfare institutions are thin, and the coalitional story dominates where they are thick. (ii) We extend the democratic-dividend literature [10] by showing that the inequality-reduction leg of the dividend is itself welfare-dependent, and by linking the size of the first-decade dividend to regime resilience two decades later. (iii) We move the education-and-democracy debate [19] from the transition margin to the resilience margin, where education operates through welfare-service stakeholding and labor-market absorption rather than values socialization alone. (iv) We provide a fully pre-registered, OWID-only research design whose falsification criteria are fixed ex ante, so that the test can adjudicate between unconditional materialist, purely coalitional, and institutionally gated accounts.\n\n## 2. Related Work\n\nTwo accounts dominate the literature on post-1990 democratic erosion, and neither tests the interaction that separates them.\n\n### 2.1 The materialist account\n\nRau and Stokes identify erosion episodes using expert-survey measures of decline in both vertical and horizontal accountability: 23 erosion spells in 22 countries between 1995 and 2020, with the average spell lasting about nine years [1]. The unit is the country-year, and the sample is democracies that were uninterrupted over the period, per the Boix-Miller-Rosato coding. The main predictor is the post-tax, post-transfer Gini coefficient. The result is strikingly monotone: predicted erosion probabilities rise from single digits in the most equal democracies to more than 30 percent in the most unequal. The memorable calibration is Sweden versus the United States. Sweden's Gini of 26.4 in 2017 predicts a 4 percent annual erosion risk; the United States' 38.4 predicts 8.4 percent; South Africa, the most unequal democracy in the sample, sits at 31 percent. Top-end concentration measured through World Inequality Database top-1 and top-10 percent shares predicts erosion equally well or better, and the bottom-50 percent share predicts the reverse. National wealth provides some insulation but is not robust across specifications. The authors run over one hundred models: different inequality measures, different structures, different controls, different units of analysis. The association survives.\n\nThe account's lineage matters for what it does not test. Houle's consolidation result, that inequality harms democratic survival but not democratization, was estimated in a global sample across the coup-driven era with discrete survival outcomes [2]. The theoretical tradition behind both is the distributional-conflict model of regimes: democratization is a commitment device that the elite accept when the revolution constraint binds, and the redistributive threat it poses is what makes elites resist [9, 10]. In that tradition, inequality is the load-bearing cause, and welfare policy is a consequence of democracy, not a condition on its survival.\n\n### 2.2 The coalitional account\n\nHaggard and Kaufman's comparative work on the post-1990 wave reaches a different conclusion [3, 15, 16]. Backsliders such as Hungary, Poland, Turkey, Venezuela, Belarus, and Russia, and survivors such as the Baltic states, Slovakia, South Korea, Taiwan, and Chile, do not separate cleanly on economic grievances. Some backsliders grew rapidly and reduced poverty; some survivors suffered deep crises. What distinguishes the two groups, in their reading, is the configuration of elites and parties: whether the political system produced a dominant coalition with incentives to dismantle constraints, and whether polarization gave that coalition an electorally sustainable base. The empirical strategy is comparative case analysis, and the authors are explicit that the economic variables that dominate the statistical literature do not carry the explanatory weight in the cases. Bermeo's conceptual history and Waldner and Lust's synthesis similarly stress steady, incremental, often stealthy executive aggrandizement as a political choice rather than an economic reflex [5, 6]. L\u00fchrmann's account of autocratization as a sequence locates the disruptive potential in institutional resilience, the general phenomenon of which the welfare state is, in our account, a specific case [22].\n\n### 2.3 The missing interaction\n\nNeither account tests the conditioning structure. The statistical account has no interaction terms at all. Its specifications include no welfare variables, so it cannot observe that the inequality coefficient is carried by the thin-welfare countries in its sample; and its sample restriction to uninterrupted democracies excludes exactly the case population that matters most for adjudication, the young democratizers that eroded. The case-based account has an interaction design in substance, backsliders versus survivors across institutional environments, but it is informal: no welfare measure is coded systematically, and no statistical claim about effect modification is made. The two accounts are therefore not in fact rivals at the level of their designs. They are main-effect and case-descriptive enterprises, each silent on the dimension that would separate them.\n\nA third literature makes the conditional structure concrete. The democratic-dividend program established that democratization increases tax revenues, secondary schooling, and structural transformation, but found no robust average effect on inequality, with suggestive heterogeneity by land inequality and structural transformation [11]. Korpi and Palme showed that welfare-state design, universal versus targeted, determines how much redistribution a given fiscal effort achieves and how much solidarity it generates [19]. Esping-Andersen's decommodification, the degree to which welfare institutions sever living standards from labor-market position, is exactly the concept of a shock absorber [17]. Pierson's policy feedback is exactly the concept of a self-defending institution [18]. What the inequality-democracy literature has never done is to put these together: to estimate the effect of an inequality shock on democratic quality as a function of the welfare institutions that preceded the shock. That is the design gap this paper fills.\n\n## 3. Theory: the welfare gate\n\n### 3.1 Definitions\n\nWe define *welfare institutions* as the universalistic service state: public health and public education spending as a share of GDP, benefiting broad segments of the population across the income distribution. This is deliberately not total social spending. Pensions, disability insurance, and targeted cash transfers dominate aggregate social-expenditure measures, and their political economy is different: they are age- or status-specific, often regressive in incidence, and they do not enroll the pivotal middle class as daily users of a public institution. The distinction is measurable. Public health and education spending is available on Our World in Data panels from WHO and World Bank sources; OECD total social spending, which we reserve as a placebo moderator, is the pensions-heavy aggregate whose gating capacity the theory denies.\n\nThe outcome is democratic quality measured continuously. The V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index (v2x_libdem, 0-1) combines electoral democracy with constraints on the executive and protection of civil liberties. For post-1990 democratizers, erosion is a graded, incremental decline in this index, executive aggrandizement and accountability erosion, not a discrete regime flip. Measuring the outcome continuously is essential: the hypothesis is about how much democracy is lost, and about erosion that stops short of authoritarian breakdown.\n\n### 3.2 The three mechanisms\n\n**Mechanism (i): automatic stabilization.** Universal health and education services are in-kind insurance against market-income shocks. When a commodity bust, a financial crisis, or a structural-transformation wave raises market inequality, the consumption of public services does not fall with income: the hospital, the school, and the university remain available. Decommodification severs the experienced standard of living from labor-market position [16]. The political consequence is that the inequality shock is attenuated before it reaches the distribution citizens experience and vote on. In thin-welfare economies, by contrast, the same market shock lands directly on private consumption and on the perceived fairness of the system, grievance forms, and the political system carries the full disturbance. The mechanism predicts a timing signature: the inequality effect on democratic quality should appear with a lag of several years, the time it takes for a shock to compound into grievance and political response, and only in the thin-welfare arm.\n\n**Mechanism (ii): constituency formation through policy feedback.** Programs create their own defenders [17]. A universal system enrolls the middle class as daily users and as taxpayers who receive visible value. That constituency holds a material stake in the integrity of public institutions: not only in the health service and the schools, but in the courts and the civil service that allocate public resources. Democratic erosion is, in its post-1990 form, the capture of precisely these institutions [5, 6]. When an incumbent begins to hollow out the civil service or subordinate the courts, the users of public services experience the attack as a threat to services they depend on, and the political cost of erosion rises. Korpi and Palme's paradox of redistribution sharpens the contrast: targeted programs, which concentrate benefits on the poor and taxes on the middle class, generate weak solidarity and are easy to cut; universal programs generate cross-class coalitions that defend themselves [18]. The mechanism predicts that the protective effect should be largest where the middle class actually uses the services, which is why a spending share is only a proxy and why the education channel matters: educated middle-class parents are the pivotal constituency of public universities and health systems.\n\n**Mechanism (iii): credible pre-commitment.** Populist equilibria arise, in the Acemoglu-Egorov-Sonin model, because voters fear that politicians may have a hidden right-wing agenda or may be captured by the rich elite. Signals of genuine left-wing conviction then become valuable, and even moderate politicians adopt populist, left-of-median policies to send them; the populist bias is larger when the value of office is high and when polarization is high [11]. Inequality feeds the fear of capture: the richer the elite, the more plausible its grip on politicians, and the more valuable the populist signal becomes. The welfare gate blocks this path at its root. Universal, automatic welfare programs pre-commit redistribution in advance: the health system, the schools, the transfers are legislated, budgeted, and delivered regardless of who wins the election. When redistribution is already institutionalized, the fear that a politician is secretly of the right is less consequential, and the electoral premium on populist promises falls. The state has, in effect, already made the credible commitment whose absence the populist promises to supply. The mechanism predicts that the gate should be strongest where welfare is universal and automatic, and weakest where welfare is discretionary and can be starved by a hostile incumbent.\n\n**Education inside the gate.** The three mechanisms give education a specific role that the values-socialization literature does not. The influential null of Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson, and Yared is that education does not cause democratization [19]. That null is about the transition margin. The welfare-gate account moves to the resilience margin: education matters for democratic survival when it is absorbed into middle-class employment and when it creates a constituency of users of public services; it matters for erosion risk when it expands without absorption. The mismatch mechanism transposes Campante and Chor's finding, that schooling combined with poor economic opportunities predicts protest, from protest onset to graded erosion [20]. Educated young people who cannot find employment commensurate with their education are precisely the shock troops of anti-system politics in the post-1990 wave. The gate therefore has two dimensions: the service state absorbs inequality shocks, and the labor market absorbs educated youth. Where both hold, education is a resilience asset; where only the first holds, the gate is partial; where neither holds, education without absorption becomes a liability.\n\n### 3.3 Hypotheses\n\nThe theory yields five pre-registered hypotheses.\n\n**H1 (the gate).** The within-country effect of a lagged inequality increase on the Liberal Democracy Index is negative and substantively large in countries with thin welfare institutions, and near zero or positive in countries with strong welfare institutions; equivalently, the interaction of inequality with pre-determined welfare strength is positive and significant.\n\n**H2 (sequencing).** Inequality surges and public-services retrenchment lead liberal-democracy declines by three to five years in thin-welfare countries, and no anticipatory welfare decline precedes erosion onset in high-welfare countries. The temporal order distinguishes the gate from the reverse causal story in which erosion causes welfare decline [22].\n\n**H3 (the welfare-dependent dividend).** Democratization reduces the top-10 percent income share and produces an inequality-reduction dividend only in high-welfare-legacy countries; the size of the first-decade dividend predicts 2010-2022 resilience.\n\n**H4 (mechanisms).** The inequality-by-thin-welfare interaction raises V-Dem polarization, and education-without-absorption, measured as ILO educated-youth unemployment, tightens the gate only where welfare is thin. Polarization is the proximate channel; the service state and the labor market are the deep parameters.\n\n**H5 (universalism contrast).** The gate is produced by public services (health and education spending), not by total social spending (pensions-heavy) and not by welfare generosity acquired later through targeted or chauvinist transfers. Total social spending functions as a placebo moderator: it does not gate.\n\nThe corollary states the asymmetry precisely. Welfare institutions built in the first democratic decade, before crises arrive, gate the inequality-erosion link. Welfare generosity purchased later by incumbents, targeted cash in Hungary, chauvinist family transfers under populist rule, is not a substitute [22, 24]. Late-bought generosity is itself part of the erosion playbook: it buys quiescence while institutions are dismantled [23, 31]. The temporal priority of universal institution-building, not the level of welfare effort, is what protects.\n\n## 4. Data and measurement\n\nThe design is restricted to public Our World in Data (OWID) panels [30]. The restriction is a feature, not a convenience: every variable in the study is downloadable by any reader, and the entire analysis is reproducible without proprietary data or expert-coding of our own. OWID aggregates the underlying primary sources, V-Dem for regime and outcome measures [29], the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform for the Gini coefficient, the World Inequality Database for top-income shares, WHO and World Bank EdStats for health and education spending, the ILO for labor-force indicators, and the OECD for the placebo moderator.\n\n**Sample.** The treated population is post-1990 democratizers: countries whose transition to electoral democracy began between 1989 and 2005, coded via the Regimes of the World (RoW) four-way classification and cross-checked against Boix-Miller-Rosato [12, 13]. RoW distinguishes closed autocracies, electoral autocracies, electoral democracies, and liberal democracies, and classifies regimes as democratic only on de facto implementation, which makes it the appropriate instrument for dating transitions in a wave full of electoral authoritarianism [12]. The sample is expected to contain 35 to 45 countries. For comparison and for the dividend analysis we also construct the full sample of all democracies over 1990-2022, which reproduces the Rau-Stokes population [1] and extends it to the young democratizers that fell below the democracy threshold, exactly the cases their sample excludes. The panel runs 1990-2022.\n\n**Outcome.** The V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index (v2x_libdem, 0-1), hosted on OWID, is the outcome in both levels and five-year differences [29]. The continuous index is essential for graded erosion: the hypothesis concerns how much democratic quality is lost within formally democratic regimes, and the post-1990 wave contains many episodes of substantial decline that stop short of breakdown. For the event-study designs we additionally define erosion onset as the first year of a sustained (three-year) decline of at least 0.03 in the index, following the graded decline thresholds used in the autocratization-measurement literature [4, 6].\n\n**Inequality treatment.** The main treatment is the lagged Gini coefficient from the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform (disposable-income where available), and the WID top-10 percent income share as the alternative treatment. Both are hosted on OWID. We lag the treatment by three years in the main specification and estimate distributed-lag dynamics to trace the 1- to 6-year profile. The top-10 percent share is the theoretically preferred measure for the populist mechanism, since the fear of elite capture in [11] is a fear of the very rich, and Rau and Stokes find top-end concentration more predictive of erosion than summary Gini measures [1]. But the Gini is the comparability workhorse, so both are reported throughout.\n\n**Welfare measure.** The gate variable is the sum of domestic general government health expenditure (percent of GDP, WHO series) and government education expenditure (percent of GDP, World Bank EdStats), both on OWID. The measure is set to its value at the end of the first democratic decade, the average over the three years centered on transition year plus ten, and is time-invariant thereafter. The pre-determination logic is the heart of the identification: the value is fixed before erosion onset (erosion, where it occurs, begins on average in the second decade after transition), it is inherited rather than chosen where communist-era or colonial-era legacies dominate, and it cannot be a consequence of the regime dynamics it is used to explain. We contrast this measure against the OECD's total social spending (percent of GDP), the pensions-heavy aggregate, as the placebo moderator for H5.\n\n**Mechanism variables.** For H4, the mediator is the V-Dem political polarization index (hosted on OWID), and the second gate dimension is the ILO educated-youth unemployment rate, youth (15-24) unemployment among those with completed education, per the Education and Mismatch Indicators on OWID. We also retrieve public-services performance series, notably the V-Dem public-service-provision or welfare-effort components where available on OWID, for the sequencing tests in H2.\n\n**Controls.** The core specifications include log GDP per capita (World Bank, via OWID), regional fixed effects, and an EU-accession indicator for the Eastern European countries. Commodity dependence is measured through natural-resource rents as a share of GDP (World Bank series on OWID) for the commodity-boom exclusion robustness check. No control is post-treatment with respect to the gate: the welfare measure is pre-determined by construction, and inequality is lagged.\n\n### 4.1 The pre-determination argument in detail\n\nThe identifying assumption deserves statement in its strongest form. Post-1990 transitions are quasi-exogenous in timing: they cluster in 1989-1991 with the collapse of the Soviet bloc, in 1992-1994 with the Southern African and Central American settlements, and in the early 2000s with the post-communist late transitions [4, 12]. At the moment of transition, welfare legacies are inherited. Eastern European democratizers walked into communist-era health and education systems of near-universal coverage; their variance in the gate variable comes from the depth and maintenance of those systems through the chaotic first decade, not from a choice about long-run welfare design made under democratic deliberation. Latin American democratizers inherited colonial-era public education skeletons of varying strength. The welfare state that gates is thus substantially outside the choice set of the first democratic governments, which is the definition of a pre-determined variable. The threat to this assumption is that the first democratic decade itself selects welfare depth: governments that consolidated well also built services. We confront this directly. First, the sequencing tests in H2 require that welfare decline follows, not precedes, erosion onset in the thin-welfare arm, which a pure selection story would not produce at the same lag structure. Second, the within-Eastern-Europe estimate holds constant the broad legacy (communism) and varies only the depth of inherited health and education systems, where the first-decade maintenance is driven by fiscal collapse and stabilization programs rather than by democratic politics. Third, the placebo moderator splits the measure: if the protective variable were really democratic-quality selection, the pension-heavy total-spending measure would gate as well; H5 predicts it does not.\n\n## 5. Estimation strategy\n\nAll estimation is implemented in Python (linearmodels and statsmodels), with standard errors clustered at the country level and wild cluster bootstrap for the interaction terms, given the small number of clusters. Six designs are pre-registered.\n\n**Design 1: the gate test (two-way fixed effects).** The core specification is\n\nLibDem_it = a_i + d_t + b1 Gini_it + b2 Gini_it x W_i + g W_i + X_it'f + e_it\n\nwhere i indexes countries, t years, a_i and d_t are country and year fixed effects, Gini is the lagged inequality treatment, W_i is the pre-determined welfare measure, and X is the control set. W_i is absorbed by the country fixed effects in its own right; the interaction is identified. The gate hypothesis is b2 > 0 and large enough that b1 + b2 W is near zero at high W and strongly negative at low W. We report the marginal effect of inequality at the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of the welfare distribution, with confidence intervals. Because two-way fixed-effects estimators with differential timing can be biased in the presence of heterogeneous effects [28], we also estimate the interacted specification on the five-year-differences version of the outcome and report Goodman-Bacon decompositions where treatment timing is involved.\n\n**Design 2: the adjudication specification.** To make the reconciliation claim directly, we estimate the baseline inequality main effect without any interaction, on the full democracy sample and on the young-democracy sample, and then introduce the interaction. The protocol commits to reading the two specifications jointly: a weak or insignificant main effect with a strong and significant interaction is the pattern that reconciles the Rau-Stokes and Haggard-Kaufman findings [1, 3], because it says the average effect hides institutional heterogeneity rather than being absent. A strong unconditional main effect that survives the interaction would instead be evidence for the unconditional materialist account.\n\n**Design 3: erosion-onset event studies and sequencing.** We stack erosion onsets among post-1990 democratizers and estimate dynamic coefficients relative to onset, separately for the high-welfare and thin-welfare arms. The event-study coefficients trace inequality and public-services spending, as well as the Liberal Democracy Index itself, in the years before and after onset. The confirmation pattern for H2 is: in the thin-welfare arm, inequality and welfare retrenchment rise before the index declines (the shock precedes the erosion); in the high-welfare arm, no such pre-onset movement appears. The lead-lag design is the primary defense against reverse causality: if erosion caused welfare decline, welfare would fall only after onset; the hypothesis requires welfare decline to lead erosion in the thin-welfare arm and to be absent in the high-welfare arm. This also separates our direction of interest from the outcome-side literature that documents how welfare states are transformed under backsliding [22].\n\n**Design 4: the democratization event study (welfare-dependent dividend).** We align countries at the transition year and estimate the dynamic path of the top-10 percent income share, public services, and education for the two decades after transition, separately by pre-determined welfare legacy (above and below the sample median). The confirmation pattern for H3 is that the top-10 percent share declines after democratization only in high-welfare-legacy countries, and that the magnitude of the first-decade decline in the top-10 percent share predicts the 2010-2022 change in the Liberal Democracy Index. This extends the democratic-dividend result [10] by conditioning the inequality-reduction leg on welfare institutions and by connecting the dividend to subsequent resilience.\n\n**Design 5: mechanism arms.** (a) Polarization channel: we estimate the effect of the inequality-by-thin-welfare interaction on the V-Dem polarization index, and then examine whether the gate effect on the Liberal Democracy Index attenuates once polarization dynamics are controlled, with the caveat that this is suggestive mediation, not causal decomposition, given that polarization is measured post-treatment. (b) Absorption channel: a triple interaction of inequality, thin welfare, and educated-youth unemployment, testing whether the gate tightens where education expands without absorption, transposing the Campante-Chor mismatch mechanism [20] from protest onset to erosion.\n\n**Design 6: robustness.** (a) Alternative inequality measures: WID top-10 percent share for the Gini, and vice versa. (b) Alternative welfare measures: health and education spending entered separately; the sum entered as a continuous variable and as a binary above/below median split. (c) Population weights. (d) Exclusion of the commodity-boom countries, identified by natural-resource rents above a threshold. (e) The within-Eastern-Europe estimate, holding the communist legacy constant. (f) Bootstrap confidence intervals for the interaction term. (g) Placebo and permutation tests on the welfare measure, including the OECD total social spending placebo for H5. Every specification is reported, including the ones that fail; the protocol contains no garden of forking paths, since the specifications and their interpretation are fixed before estimation.\n\n[FIGURE:fig2]\n\n## 6. Expected results and falsification criteria\n\nThe protocol commits ex ante to the following inference rules, so that the test can adjudicate between the accounts.\n\n**Confirmation** of the welfare-gate hypothesis requires all five conditions. (a) A significant positive interaction between lagged inequality and pre-determined welfare strength on liberal-democracy trajectories, with the within-country inequality effect near zero or positive in the high-welfare arm and strongly negative in the thin-welfare arm, robust to every measure and sample swap in Design 6. (b) Sequencing: inequality surges and public-services retrenchment lead liberal-democracy declines by three to five years in thin-welfare countries, with no anticipatory welfare decline before erosion onset in the high-welfare arm (Design 3). (c) The welfare-dependent dividend: democratization reduces the top-10 percent income share only in high-welfare-legacy countries, and the size of the first-decade dividend predicts 2010-2022 resilience (Design 4). (d) The mechanism arms: the inequality-by-thin-welfare interaction raises V-Dem polarization, and education-without-absorption tightens the gate only where welfare is thin (Design 5). (e) The universalism contrast: public services gate, OECD total social spending does not (Design 6g).\n\n**Disconfirmation** is equally sharp. If the inequality effect is homogeneous across welfare arms, if the interaction is insignificant or of the wrong sign in the core specification, if the sequencing is reversed (erosion precedes welfare decline), or if the interaction collapses once GDP level, region, and EU accession are controlled, the hypothesis as stated is falsified. Each of those outcomes has a clear interpretation in the literature. A homogeneous inequality effect across arms favors the unconditional materialist account [1, 2]. A reversed sequence, with welfare decline following erosion, favors the outcome-side transformation literature [22] over the gate. A collapsed interaction favors the purely coalitional account [3]. The design is a genuine three-way adjudication, not a confirmation exercise. We also pre-commit to the marginal-effect reporting standard: the gate claim lives or dies on the inequality marginal effect at the welfare-distribution percentiles, not on the interaction coefficient alone, because a significant interaction with a negative marginal effect everywhere would not constitute a gate.\n\n[FIGURE:fig3]\n\n## 7. Discussion\n\nThe welfare-gate hypothesis is offered as a resolution to a dispute that has been stuck because its two protagonists estimate different objects. The value of the design lies in what each possible outcome would teach. We discuss the three central readings before the data arrive.\n\n**Reconciling the two accounts.** If H1 and H2 hold, the Rau-Stokes inequality effect [1] and the Haggard-Kaufman economic skepticism [3] are not in tension. The inequality effect in the global sample is carried by the thin-welfare democracies: the post-communist laggards, the Latin American service-skeletons, the Southern African cases where public services reach only part of the population. In the high-welfare arm, inequality rises without erosion, which is why close comparison of cases like the Baltic states, where inequality rose substantially after 2008 without producing democratic collapse, finds no economic story. The case-based account studied mostly the thin-welfare backsliders, Hungary, Poland, Turkey, Venezuela, and the materialist account studied mostly the pooled average. Both were right about their effective samples, and wrong about the population. The gate explains the pattern in the countries where the two literatures collide: Hungary and Poland are the crucial cases because they are the exception that tests the rule. Both had substantial communist-era welfare states, but of the wrong structure: pension-heavy, service-thin. In the framework of this paper, their first democratic decade consolidated the pension component while health and education systems atrophied under fiscal pressure, so the middle class was never enrolled in the service state as a daily, defended public institution. The gate was never built. Vanhuysse's account of early post-communist social policy as strategic demobilization [23], and the documentation of how Hungarian and Polish welfare states were converted into instruments of the illiberal project [22, 31], are the outcome side of the same coin: a welfare state that does not gate is available for capture.\n\n**The democratic dividend, conditioned.** The most consequential extension is to the democratic-dividend literature. Acemoglu, Naidu, Restrepo, and Robinson established that democratization raises taxation and schooling but found no robust average inequality reduction, with heterogeneity they could not fully explain [10]. The welfare-gate account supplies the missing conditioner: the inequality-reduction leg of the dividend materializes only where universal service institutions are strong enough to convert fiscal expansion into distributional change. In thin-welfare democratizers, higher taxation without service delivery, or with leakage, produces neither redistribution nor a middle-class constituency attached to public provision. The first-decade dividend, or its absence, is then the mechanism that connects democratization to its own fate: countries whose first democratic decade did not deliver the visible, universal dividend entered the crisis years with no welfare buffer and no service constituency, precisely the configuration that H1 predicts erodes under inequality pressure. If H3 and H4 hold, the dividend literature and the erosion literature are one literature: the dividend is the resilience mechanism, and its failure is the erosion mechanism. This also reframes the education-and-democracy null [19]: education produces democratic resilience not through values socialization but through absorption into middle-class employment and enrollment in public services. Where education expands without absorption, the Campante-Chor mismatch [20] operates, and the educated young become an erosion resource rather than a democratic one. The cleavage-structure results of Gethin, Martinez-Toledano, and Piketty [25] and the redistributive politics of education in Ansell [26] are the microfoundations of that channel.\n\n**The universalism contrast and the policy reading.** The sharpest claim in the paper is H5: total social spending and late-bought generosity do not gate. If H5 holds, the policy implication is not \"spend more on welfare\" but \"build universal service institutions early.\" For any future democratization wave, the testable prescription is that the first democratic decade is the window in which universal health and education systems must be constructed, because legitimacy and constituency are built by the institutions that exist when the first crisis arrives. Welfare effort purchased later, targeted cash, chauvinist family allowances, functions as pacification [23] and as an instrument of the eroding incumbent [22, 24]. The distinction between universal services and total social spending is the distinction between institutions that create their own defenders [17, 18] and expenditures that buy quiescence.\n\n## 8. Limitations\n\nFour limitations are intrinsic to the design, and we state them as such rather than as future work.\n\n**Small N and statistical power.** The treated sample is 35 to 45 countries, and the interaction is a difference-in-differences of a difference-in-differences: the effective variation is the within-country association between inequality and liberal democracy, compared across welfare arms. Power for interaction tests is low in samples of this size, and the clustered standard errors rest on a modest number of clusters. We mitigate with wild cluster bootstrap inference, with the five-year-differences specification, and with the event-study designs, but the study is powered for large conditional effects and will not detect a weak gate. The design is honest about this: the falsification criteria in Section 6 are stated for the effects the theory itself predicts to be large.\n\n**The welfare measure is a proxy.** Public health and education spending as a share of GDP measures fiscal effort, not universality, not quality, and not usage by the middle class. Two countries with identical spending shares can differ in whether public hospitals serve the well-off or only the poor, and the mechanism in H1 is about usage. The proxy bias is conservative: measurement error in the gate variable attenuates the interaction and biases against confirmation. The within-Eastern-Europe design and the placebo moderator partially discipline the proxy, but the ideal test would require usage data that OWID panels do not carry. We flag the distinction between the theoretical construct, universality, and the measured variable, spending, as the design's most consequential approximation.\n\n**Identification of the gate.** The welfare measure is pre-determined relative to erosion onset, but it is not randomly assigned. The first democratic decade is itself a period of democratic politics, and governments that consolidated well also maintained services. The sequencing tests, the within-Eastern-Europe estimate, and the placebo contrast each address a specific version of this threat, but none eliminates the possibility that a third factor, state capacity, geography, or geopolitical alignment, drives both welfare maintenance and democratic resilience. The EU-accession process is the most salient such factor for the Eastern European cases, which is why the within-Eastern-Europe estimate and the EU-accession control are built into the protocol rather than consigned to robustness; it remains the case that EU conditionality was itself a welfare-building force in the first decade, which means the gate and the accession channel are partially entangled by construction.\n\n**Measurement of the outcome and the treatment.** The Liberal Democracy Index is expert-coded, and its inter-temporal comparability is contested [6]. The Gini coefficient's cross-country comparability is limited by differing underlying surveys and income concepts, and the PIP harmonization, while the best available, does not remove the issue. Both biases are plausibly classical in this design, attenuating main effects and interactions alike, but the threat to the sequencing tests is asymmetric: if erosion onset is misdated, the lead-lag structure in Design 3 shifts, and the confirmation pattern for H2 could be manufactured by measurement timing. We address this by the three-year sustained-decline coding rule, by robustness to alternative onset codings, and by the requirement that the sequencing pattern differ across welfare arms, which a pure measurement artifact would not produce.\n\n## 9. Conclusion\n\nThe post-1990 democratizers are the population on which the dispute about democratic erosion should be adjudicated, and they are the population the global statistical literature has excluded. This paper has argued that the adjudicating variable is the welfare state, specifically the universal service state built in the first democratic decade. The hypothesis is precise: inequality erodes young democracies only where welfare institutions are too thin to absorb and convert it, and the inequality-reduction leg of the democratic dividend itself materializes only behind the gate. The design is fixed: an OWID-only panel, a pre-determined welfare measure, a two-way fixed-effects interaction, event studies for sequencing, and a commitment to report every specification, including the ones that fail. If the evidence confirms the gate, the reconciliation of the materialist and coalitional accounts is institutional: inequality matters, but its effect is conditional on institutions that half the post-1990 wave never built. If it disconfirms, the unconditional accounts stand, and the adjudication is still progress. Either way, the study moves the debate from the unobservable average to the conditional structure that the two leading accounts have spent a decade talking past.\n\n## References\n\n[1] Rau, Eli G., and Susan Stokes. 2025. \"Income Inequality and the Erosion of Democracy in the Twenty-First Century.\" *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* 122(1): e2422543121.\n\n[2] Houle, Christian. 2009. \"Inequality and Democracy: Why Inequality Harms Consolidation but Does Not Affect Democratization.\" *World Politics* 61(4): 589-622.\n\n[3] Haggard, Stephan, and Robert R.
